title: Growing basil microgreens
subtitle: Warm-loving herb microgreens with a sweet anise note, cut in 10 to 14 days
excerpt: Basil microgreens require warmth above other microgreen crops and take 10 to 14 days on a 25 cm tray. The cotyledons have a sweet, anise-forward flavour typical of mature basil, and are used in salads, pasta, and as a pizza topping.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Penn State Extension indoor herb growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The gel layer that forms around basil seeds when they are exposed to water. Basil seeds are mucilaginous: when wet, each seed quickly develops a transparent gelatinous coating. This is a normal property of the seed and aids germination, but can cause problems in microgreen growing if seeds are pre-soaked or surface-watered.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Basil microgreens are a warm-loving indoor crop that takes 10 to 14 days on a 25 cm tray. Sow dry (not pre-soaked), blackout for two to three days, then move to a warm bright position for the remaining 7 to 11 days until the cotyledons are fully open. The flavour is sweet and aromatic, characteristic of mature basil.
Basil needs warmth more than most microgreen crops; it sulks below 18°C and fails below 15°C. In summer a sunny kitchen counter is ideal. In winter, keep the tray in the warmest room in the house.

Light: a very bright south-facing windowsill in summer works well. In winter and spring, a grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours per day is strongly recommended. Basil microgreens in low light produce pale, spindly cotyledons with poor flavour.

Temperature: 20 to 25°C. This is higher than most other microgreen crops. Basil seed germinates poorly below 18°C; the cotyledons fail to develop normally below 16°C. A heated propagator set at 22°C solves the winter temperature problem during germination; after the shoots emerge, a warm windowsill or grow-light shelf maintains the growing temperature.

Day 0: sow dry. Basil seed is mucilaginous: when wet, each seed quickly develops a gel coating. Do not pre-soak basil seed. Fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter basil seed sparingly at 10 to 15 g per 25 cm tray; the seeds expand when they absorb moisture from the medium and need slightly more space than brassica seed. Press gently into contact with the medium.

Days 1 to 3: blackout. Cover lightly (a second tray without weight, or just a sheet of black plastic). Basil shoots are finer than brassica shoots and a heavy weighted cover can damage the emerging seedlings. Remove when the majority of shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall.

Day 4 onward: light and warmth. Basil microgreens need both bright light and warm temperatures simultaneously; a grow-light shelf in a warm room is the best setup in winter. The cotyledons green up within 24 to 48 hours in a warm, bright position.

Watering: bottom-water only. Basil seedlings are more sensitive to surface moisture than brassicas; top-watering causes rapid damping off. Set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 cm of water and let the medium absorb it from below.

Days 10 to 14: cut. When cotyledons are fully open and 4 to 6 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium surface with scissors. Use fresh immediately for the best flavour; basil microgreens wilt more quickly than brassica cotyledons. Refrigerate for up to one day in a sealed container.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on basil microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Seedlings collapse and rot at the base within the first few days
items.cause: Damping off, more common in basil than in brassicas.
items.fix: Bottom-water only; top-watering basil seedlings is the most common cause of failure. Ensure airflow around the tray. Basil is the most susceptible microgreen to damping off; the precautions are non-negotiable.

items.symptom: Seedlings fail to emerge or germinate very slowly beyond day 5
items.cause: Room too cold, or seeds buried too deep.
items.fix: Raise the temperature above 20°C. Basil seed should rest on the medium surface or just below it; burying the seed slows germination.

items.symptom: Cotyledons fail to green up or stay yellow after moving to light
items.fix: Warm the room and move to a brighter position or add a grow light. Cold basil microgreens develop slowly and may yellow rather than green up.

items.symptom: Stems leggy and weak, cotyledons small
items.cause: Insufficient light, or temperature too low.
items.fix: Basil microgreens need both light and warmth. A grow light without adequate warmth, or warmth without adequate light, both produce poor results.

content.text: Standard vegetable basil seed (sweet basil, Genovese) works for microgreen growing. Use untreated seed. Do not pre-soak basil seed; the gel coating makes handling difficult and the seeds stick together in clumps.
